summary: This talk provides a speed-run through graph fundamentals for AI builders. Ainge begins with graph basics: nodes (vertices) connected by edges (relationships), with types, labels, properties, and direction. The core focus is building better graphs from unstructured text. Starting with naive triple extraction (subject-predicate-object), Ainge demonstrates that giving the extractor a structured schema—e.g., a recipe with ingredients, quantities, and steps—produces far more meaningful results than undirected triple extraction. Further ontological refinements, such as standardizing ingredient names and metric units, improve queryability and matching. Entity deduplication addresses the problem where variants like garlic cloves and minced garlic should unify. While naive retrospective matching requires knowing all entities in advance, embedding models enable flexible matching of unknown terms, exemplifying hybrid graph-plus-AI approaches. The talk then covers three graph-native algorithms. Personalized PageRank (PPR), a variant of Google's PageRank from 1998, simulates a random walker that marks nodes and teleports back to a starting node, surfacing nodes with strong relationships to the origin. Ainge references the Pinterest Pixie paper and HippoRag, and demonstrates PPR finding landmark legal cases like Miranda v. Arizona through citation graphs. Shortest path algorithms find the most direct route between two known nodes, useful for explaining relationships such as tracing why code broke after a change. On a .NET codebase, this technique achieved 40% reduction in code search tool calls. Variants include K-shortest paths and weighted cheapest paths. Subgraph matching queries entirely on relationship structure, finding patterns like decorator patterns in code without knowing specific instances—an enabling capability difficult to replicate with other tools. The talk closes by noting that search algorithms for dependencies and networks are more run-of-the-mill, and that prediction, similarity, and clustering—topics not covered today—edge into GraphRAG, dynamic graphs, and schema-less graph territory where things get super interesting. References and pointers will be in the presentation pack. Throughout, Ainge emphasizes that graph techniques complement AI-age problems in search, pattern recognition, retrieval, and knowledge management, encouraging practitioners to use graph-native or hybrid algorithms for smarter, cheaper, and more reliable AI applications.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction & Motivation
sections.summary: Ainge introduces the talk's motivation: graphs are powerful but often misapplied, leading to a valley of despair. The talk focuses on underlying graph patterns for AI builders, not GraphRAG or agent memory graphs specifically.

sections.title: Graph Basics
sections.summary: Speed-run definition of graphs: nodes (vertices) and edges (relationships), with types, labels, properties, and direction.

sections.title: Extracting Graphs from Unstructured Text
sections.summary: Basic triple extraction (subject-predicate-object) from a recipe produces a graph but with limited usefulness due to lack of structure.

sections.title: Schema-First Approach
sections.summary: Giving the extractor a structured schema (recipe with ingredients, quantities, steps) yields far more meaningful and tidy graphs with consistent, interrogable node and edge types.

sections.title: Ontological Improvements
sections.summary: Ontology describes what to extract into the structure. Instructions to standardize ingredient names and metric units are as important as the schema itself for matching and conversion.

sections.title: Entity Matching & Deduplication
sections.summary: Addresses the potato/potato problem where variant names like garlic cloves and minced garlic should unify. Naive retrospective matching requires knowing all entities in advance; embedding models enable flexible matching of unknown terms, combining graph and AI techniques.

sections.title: Graph Query: Cypher vs SQL
sections.summary: Simple recipe query comparing Cypher graph query with SQL. Graph queries naturally excel at traversing multiple relationships where SQL becomes unwieldy.

sections.title: Personalized PageRank
sections.summary: PPR variant of PageRank simulates a random walker marking nodes and teleporting back to a starting node, surfacing nodes with strong relationships to the origin. References Pinterest Pixie paper and HippoRag. Real-world example: finding Miranda v. Arizona through Supreme Court citation graph relationships.

sections.title: Shortest Path Algorithm
sections.summary: Finds most direct route between two known nodes. Example: tracing why checkout code broke after changing basket constructor. Variants include K-shortest paths and weighted cheapest paths. .NET evaluation showed 40% reduction in code search tool calls.

sections.title: Subgraph Matching
sections.summary: Queries entirely on relationship structure to find patterns without knowing specific instances. Example: finding decorator pattern in eShop codebase. Described as an enabling algorithm rather than optimization, useful for anti-patterns, security issues, and legal argument discovery.

sections.title: Conclusion & Future Directions
sections.summary: Closes by noting search algorithms for dependencies and networks are more run-of-the-mill. Mentions prediction, similarity, and clustering as topics not covered today that edge into GraphRAG, dynamic graphs, and schema-less graph territory—deliberately excluded but where things get super interesting. References will be in the presentation pack. Ainge hopes the concepts inspire use of graph-native or hybrid algorithms for smarter, cheaper, and more reliable AI applications.

Recipe query: Cypher vs SQL comparison for finding recipes containing garlic

Shortest path: tracing why checkout code broke after changing basket constructor via code graph traversal

Even the best prompts are not bulletproof for standardizing outputs
